dbms-ops-security:0.prompt: A team runs dashboards that aggregate two years of orders directly on the primary PostgreSQL OLTP database, and checkout latency spikes whenever they refresh. What is the core mismatch?
options: The OLTP database lacks enough B-tree indexes, so adding an index per dashboard filter will fix it
A row-oriented OLTP store tuned for short point reads/writes is serving long scans over many rows, competing for I/O, CPU and buffer cache
PostgreSQL cannot compute GROUP BY over more than a year of data without partitioning
Dashboards use read-committed isolation, which blocks concurrent checkout writes
dbms-ops-security:0.explanation: OLTP engines store whole rows together and are optimised for many small transactions; analytical scans read huge row ranges and evict hot pages, hurting checkout. Moving analytics to a columnar OLAP store (or at least a separate system) is the fix. Adding indexes doesn't help full-range aggregations and slows writes; readers don't block writers under MVCC.

dbms-ops-security:0.prompt: In a star schema for e-commerce sales, which of these belongs in the fact table?
options: The customer's shipping address and loyalty tier
The product's category name and brand
Quantity and revenue per order line, with foreign keys to date, product and customer dimensions
The calendar month name and fiscal quarter label
dbms-ops-security:0.explanation: Fact tables hold numeric measures at a declared grain plus foreign keys to dimensions. Descriptive attributes (address, category, month name) live in dimension tables so they can be used for filtering and grouping without repeating them on every fact row.

dbms-ops-security:0.prompt: You snowflake a product dimension into product → subcategory → category tables. What is the main trade-off versus keeping a single denormalized product dimension (star)?
options: Less redundancy and easier maintenance of category attributes, at the cost of extra joins in most analytical queries
Faster queries because the dimension tables are smaller, with no real downside
It allows the fact table to drop its product foreign key
It converts additive measures into semi-additive ones
dbms-ops-security:0.explanation: Snowflaking normalizes dimensions: category names are stored once, but queries that group by category must now join through extra tables. Smaller dimension tables rarely matter because dimensions are tiny compared with facts, so 'faster with no downside' is the tempting but wrong choice.

dbms-ops-security:0.prompt: When designing a new fact table for a warehouse, which decision should be made first because the others depend on it?
options: Which BI tool will query it
Which columns to compress
Which dimensions get surrogate keys
The grain: exactly what one fact row represents (e.g. one order line)
dbms-ops-security:0.explanation: Kimball-style modelling declares the grain first; the grain determines which dimensions apply and which measures are valid. Choosing dimensions or keys before the grain often produces mixed-grain facts that double count when aggregated.

dbms-ops-security:0.prompt: Why does a columnar OLAP engine answer `SELECT region, SUM(revenue) FROM sales GROUP BY region` over billions of rows much faster than a row store?
options: It keeps every row in memory permanently
It reads only the region and revenue columns, which are stored contiguously and compress very well, so far less data is scanned
It builds a B-tree index on every column automatically
It skips MVCC visibility checks by running without transactions
dbms-ops-security:0.explanation: Columnar storage lets the engine read just the referenced columns, and similar values stored together compress heavily (run-length, dictionary encoding), often enabling vectorised execution. It is not about keeping everything in memory or indexing every column.

dbms-ops-security:0.prompt: A customer moves from Pune to Delhi. Analysts want past sales still attributed to Pune and new sales to Delhi. How should the customer dimension handle this?
options: Overwrite the city in place (Type 1) and recompute history
Store the city on every fact row instead of in the dimension
Insert a new dimension row with a new surrogate key and effective-from/to dates (Type 2); new facts reference the new key
Delete the old customer row and re-insert it with the new city
dbms-ops-security:0.explanation: A Type 2 slowly changing dimension keeps history by versioning the dimension row; old facts keep pointing at the Pune version's surrogate key. Type 1 overwriting is simpler but rewrites history, so all past sales would suddenly show Delhi.

dbms-ops-security:0.prompt: In PostgreSQL, you move long analytical queries to a hot-standby streaming replica. What operational problem is most likely to appear?
options: The replica rejects SELECT statements longer than 30 seconds by default
Long queries can conflict with WAL replay: they get cancelled, or with hot_standby_feedback on, the primary delays vacuum and bloats
Analytical queries on the replica take row locks that block writes on the primary
The replica becomes columnar and can no longer serve OLTP failover
dbms-ops-security:0.explanation: Replay may need to remove row versions a standby query still sees; PostgreSQL then cancels the query after max_standby_streaming_delay, or hot_standby_feedback makes the primary keep dead tuples (bloat). Standby queries cannot lock rows on the primary, so that distractor is wrong.

dbms-ops-security:0.prompt: Which are typical characteristics of OLAP workloads? Select all that apply.
options: Large scans that aggregate many rows
Columnar storage and compression
Denormalized star or snowflake schemas
High-concurrency single-row updates with strict millisecond latency
Strict 3NF modelling chosen mainly to avoid update anomalies
dbms-ops-security:0.explanation: OLAP is read-heavy aggregation over history, so it favours columnar storage and denormalized dimensional models. Many tiny latency-sensitive updates and 3NF modelling to prevent update anomalies are OLTP traits.

dbms-ops-security:0.prompt: Which statements about fact table measures are correct? Select all that apply.
options: Revenue per order line is additive: it can be summed across every dimension
An account balance snapshot is semi-additive: summing it across time is meaningless
Fact tables are usually the largest tables in a warehouse
Fact tables should store long descriptive text such as product names for faster filtering
A ratio like profit margin should be stored and summed directly rather than recomputed from its parts
dbms-ops-security:0.explanation: Additive measures sum across all dimensions; balances can be summed across accounts but not across days. Facts dominate warehouse size. Descriptive text belongs in dimensions, and ratios are non-additive, so you sum numerator and denominator then divide.

dbms-ops-security:0.prompt: When data reaches the warehouse through a scheduled ETL/ELT pipeline, OLAP reports are usually somewhat behind the OLTP source.
options: True
False
dbms-ops-security:0.explanation: Batch or micro-batch pipelines introduce latency between a transaction committing and it being visible in the warehouse. Change-data-capture can shrink this lag but rarely to zero.

dbms-ops-security:0.prompt: A snowflake schema generally needs fewer joins than the equivalent star schema.
options: True
False
dbms-ops-security:0.explanation: False. Snowflaking splits dimensions into normalized sub-tables, so queries need more joins to reach attributes like category. A star keeps each dimension in one table, one join from the fact.

dbms-ops-security:1.prompt: With this node-postgres code, which value of `email` makes the query return every user?
dbms-ops-security:1.code:
const sql = "SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = '" + email + "'";
const { rows } = await db.query(sql);
options: admin@example.com
NULL
dbms-ops-security:1.explanation: The input closes the string literal and appends `OR '1'='1'`, which is always true, so the WHERE matches all rows. `%` would only matter with LIKE, and `NULL` is just compared as the text 'NULL'.

dbms-ops-security:1.prompt: In node-postgres, why does `db.query('SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = $1', [email])` prevent SQL injection?
options: The driver escapes quotes in `email` before splicing it into the SQL text
PostgreSQL rejects any parameter containing a quote character
The SQL text and the values are sent separately; the value is bound after parsing, so it can never be interpreted as SQL
The query runs in a read-only transaction
dbms-ops-security:1.explanation: With parameters, node-postgres uses the extended query protocol: the statement is parsed with placeholders, then values are bound as data. Client-side escaping is a different (weaker) technique some libraries use; quotes in values are allowed and stored as-is.

dbms-ops-security:1.prompt: An API lets clients pick a sort column (`?sort=created_at`). What is the safe way to put it into a PostgreSQL query?
options: Bind it as a `$2` placeholder in `ORDER BY $2`
Escape it by doubling any single quotes
Wrap it in single quotes before concatenating
Map it through an allowlist of known column names and only interpolate the mapped identifier
dbms-ops-security:1.explanation: Placeholders bind values, not identifiers, so `ORDER BY $2` sorts by a constant rather than the column. Quote-doubling and quoting are for string literals and don't make identifiers safe. An allowlist (or a dedicated identifier-quoting helper) is the reliable fix.

dbms-ops-security:1.prompt: A search endpoint uses `WHERE name LIKE $1` with the value `'%' + input + '%'`. A user submits `%_%`. What happens?
options: SQL injection: the user can run arbitrary statements
Not injection, but `%` and `_` act as wildcards, so the user can match everything and trigger expensive scans; escape them if literal matching is intended
PostgreSQL throws a syntax error because `_` is reserved
The parameter is treated as a regex and fails
dbms-ops-security:1.explanation: The value is still bound safely, so no SQL can be injected, but LIKE interprets `%` and `_` inside the pattern. Escape them (e.g. with a backslash, PostgreSQL's default LIKE escape) when users should match literal characters.

dbms-ops-security:1.prompt: A signup form stores the username `x'; DROP TABLE audit;--` safely using parameters. Weeks later a nightly report job builds `"... WHERE owner = '" + row.username + "'"` and the audit table disappears. What is this called?
options: Second-order SQL injection: trusted-looking data from the database is later concatenated into SQL
Blind SQL injection via timing
A race condition between the signup and the report job
Cross-site scripting stored in the database
dbms-ops-security:1.explanation: Second-order injection happens when stored data is treated as safe because it came from your own database. Every query must be parameterized regardless of where values come from. It is not blind/timing-based and not XSS, which targets browsers.

dbms-ops-security:1.prompt: A PL/pgSQL function runs `EXECUTE 'SELECT count(*) FROM ' || tbl || ' WHERE status = ''' || st || '''';`. How should it be fixed?
options: It's already safe because it runs inside a stored function
Mark the function SECURITY DEFINER
Use `EXECUTE format('SELECT count(*) FROM %I WHERE status = $1', tbl) USING st`
Wrap the whole string in quote_literal()
dbms-ops-security:1.explanation: Dynamic SQL inside functions is just as injectable as in app code. `format` with `%I` quotes the identifier and `USING` binds the value as a parameter. SECURITY DEFINER makes things worse (runs with owner rights), and quote_literal on the whole statement would turn it into a string.

dbms-ops-security:1.prompt: An Express login handler runs `users.findOne({ email: req.body.email, password: req.body.password })` against MongoDB. An attacker posts JSON `{"email":"a@b.com","password":{"$ne":null}}`. What's the best fix?
options: Validate the body with a schema (e.g. zod) so both fields must be strings, and compare a password hash in code
Switch to `find` instead of `findOne`
Use HTTPS so the payload can't be modified
Wrap the query in a try/catch
dbms-ops-security:1.explanation: This is NoSQL operator injection: the object `{ $ne: null }` matches any password. Enforcing string types removes operators, and passwords should be hashed and verified with bcrypt/argon2 anyway. HTTPS protects transport, not malicious clients.

dbms-ops-security:1.prompt: Which measures prevent SQL injection or limit its damage? Select all that apply.
options: Parameterized queries for all values
Running the app with a least-privilege database role
Allowlisting user-chosen identifiers like sort columns
HTML-encoding values when rendering pages
Serving the API over HTTPS
dbms-ops-security:1.explanation: Parameters stop values being parsed as SQL, allowlists cover identifiers, and least privilege limits what an injected statement can do. HTML encoding targets XSS, and HTTPS protects data in transit; neither stops a malicious input reaching the SQL parser.

dbms-ops-security:1.prompt: Which of these Node.js calls are vulnerable to SQL injection when `id` and `table` come from the request? Select all that apply.
options: pg: db.query('SELECT * FROM t WHERE id = $1', [id])
pg: db.query(`SELECT * FROM t WHERE id = ${id}`)
pg: db.query('SELECT * FROM ' + table + ' WHERE id = $1', [id])
pg: db.query({ text: 'SELECT * FROM t WHERE id = $1', values: [id] })
postgres.js: sql`SELECT * FROM t WHERE id = ${id}`
dbms-ops-security:1.explanation: A plain template literal is string concatenation, and binding `id` doesn't protect the concatenated `table`. postgres.js tagged templates turn `${}` into bound parameters, so that one is safe despite looking similar, as are both forms of pg's `$1` binding.

dbms-ops-security:1.prompt: Using an ORM guarantees that an application is immune to SQL injection.
options: True
False
dbms-ops-security:1.explanation: False. ORMs parameterize their generated queries, but raw-query escape hatches, string-built where clauses and dynamic identifiers can still be injectable if developers concatenate input.

dbms-ops-security:1.prompt: A prepared statement lets the database parse a query once and execute it repeatedly with different bound values.
options: True
False
dbms-ops-security:1.explanation: True. Prepared statements separate parsing/planning from execution; values are supplied at execute time. That separation is also why bound values cannot change the statement's structure.

dbms-ops-security:2.prompt: Your managed PostgreSQL has storage encryption at rest enabled. Which threat does this mainly protect against?
options: An attacker who has stolen the app's database credentials
SQL injection that dumps the users table
Someone obtaining the raw disks, volume snapshots or backup files without the keys
A DBA running SELECT on sensitive columns
dbms-ops-security:2.explanation: Encryption at rest is transparent to anyone who can connect and query; data is decrypted for them. It protects media: stolen drives, leaked snapshots or backups. Credential theft and injection go through the normal query path, so they are unaffected.

dbms-ops-security:2.prompt: A Node service connects to PostgreSQL with `sslmode=require` and no root certificate configured. What does this give you?
options: Encryption and full verification of the server's certificate and hostname
Encryption, but no verification of the server's identity, so a man-in-the-middle can still impersonate the database
No encryption; `require` only checks that the server supports TLS
Mutual TLS with a client certificate
dbms-ops-security:2.explanation: In libpq-compatible clients, `require` encrypts the channel but (without a root CA) does not validate the certificate. Use `verify-full` with the CA to check both the chain and that the hostname matches. Client certificates are a separate setting.

dbms-ops-security:2.prompt: You encrypt `ssn` in the application with randomized AES-GCM before storing it. What capability do you lose?
options: The ability to back up the table
The ability to use TLS to the database
The ability to store the column as bytea
The ability to index, search or range-query that column in SQL, since the database only sees random-looking ciphertext
dbms-ops-security:2.explanation: Randomized encryption produces different ciphertext for the same value each time, so the database can't compare, index or sort plaintext. Backups and TLS are unaffected, and bytea is a fine storage type for ciphertext.

dbms-ops-security:2.prompt: With envelope encryption, each record is encrypted with a data key, and data keys are encrypted by a master key in KMS. Why is this design popular?
options: Rotating the master key only requires re-wrapping the small data keys, and bulk encryption happens locally without sending data to KMS
It makes data searchable while encrypted
It removes the need for access control on the KMS
It lets the master key be stored safely in the same table as the data
dbms-ops-security:2.explanation: KMS only encrypts/decrypts small data keys, so large payloads never leave your service and master key rotation is cheap. It does not make ciphertext searchable, and the master key must stay in KMS behind strict IAM, never beside the data.

dbms-ops-security:2.prompt: Support staff must look up customers by exact national ID, which must stay encrypted. Which design best balances lookup and leakage?
options: Store the ID in plaintext but restrict access with a view
Deterministic encryption only, so equal IDs produce equal ciphertext
Randomized encryption of the value plus a separate keyed HMAC ('blind index') column used for equality lookups
Hash the ID with unsalted SHA-256 and index the hash
dbms-ops-security:2.explanation: A keyed HMAC supports exact-match lookups without revealing the value, while the randomized ciphertext holds the data. Unsalted SHA-256 of a small ID space is brute-forceable without a key, and deterministic encryption also enables lookups but makes every copy of the value identical everywhere.

dbms-ops-security:2.prompt: Where should the keys used for application-level column encryption be kept?
options: In a KMS or secrets manager, fetched at runtime with tightly scoped IAM
In a `keys` table in the same database
Hard-coded in the repository so every environment matches
In `.env.example` so new developers can run the app
dbms-ops-security:2.explanation: Keys stored with the data (same DB) or in the repo are exposed by the same breach the encryption is meant to survive. A KMS/secret manager separates key access from data access and supports rotation and audit.

dbms-ops-security:2.prompt: In PostgreSQL, a developer calls `pgp_sym_encrypt(card, 'S3cretKey!')` with the key as a literal in the SQL text. What's the biggest risk?
options: pgcrypto cannot encrypt text values
The key can appear in server statement logs, error logs or monitoring that capture query text
The encrypted output is longer than the column allows
The function silently stores plaintext when the key is shorter than 16 characters
dbms-ops-security:2.explanation: Server-side encryption means the key travels to and is visible to the database, including in logs when statement logging or error reporting records query text. App-side encryption keeps keys out of the database. pgcrypto handles text fine.

dbms-ops-security:2.prompt: What does TLS between your Node app and the database protect against? Select all that apply.
options: Eavesdropping on queries and results on the network
Tampering with traffic in transit
SQL injection from malicious request bodies
A compromised database superuser reading table data
Impersonation of the server, when certificates are verified
dbms-ops-security:2.explanation: TLS provides confidentiality and integrity in transit, plus server authentication when you verify certificates. Injection arrives inside legitimate encrypted queries, and anyone with DB privileges sees decrypted data.

dbms-ops-security:2.prompt: Which statements about encryption at rest are correct? Select all that apply.
options: Cloud-managed disk encryption is transparent to SQL queries
Backups and snapshots need encryption too, either inherited or configured separately
It prevents a user with SELECT privileges from reading plaintext
It removes the need for database access control
dbms-ops-security:2.explanation: Storage encryption is applied below the database, so queries are unchanged, and backups must be covered as well. It does nothing against authorized query access, so access control remains essential.

dbms-ops-security:2.prompt: Passwords hashed with bcrypt or argon2 are encrypted, so an admin holding the right key can decrypt them back to plaintext.
options: True
False
dbms-ops-security:2.explanation: False. These are one-way, salted, deliberately slow hash functions. You verify a password by hashing the attempt and comparing; nothing can decrypt them. Encryption is reversible by design, which is why it's wrong for passwords.

dbms-ops-security:2.prompt: Even with TLS to the database and encrypted storage, the database server process works with plaintext values in memory while executing queries.
options: True
False
dbms-ops-security:2.explanation: True. TLS ends at the server and storage encryption is undone when pages are read. Only application-side (client-side) encryption keeps values opaque to the database server itself.

dbms-ops-security:3.prompt: You need to rename `users.fullname` to `display_name` on a busy service with rolling deploys and no downtime. What's the safest approach?
options: Run `ALTER TABLE users RENAME COLUMN` and deploy the new code at the same moment
Expand/contract: add `display_name`, dual-write, backfill, switch reads, then drop `fullname` in a later release
Create a new table, copy everything, and swap names during a maintenance window
Rename the column and rely on the ORM to map the old name automatically
dbms-ops-security:3.explanation: During a rolling deploy old and new code run together, so the schema must work for both. Expand/contract keeps both columns valid until no code uses the old one. A direct rename breaks whichever version isn't expecting it.

dbms-ops-security:3.prompt: In PostgreSQL, adding an index to a large hot table with plain `CREATE INDEX` causes write timeouts. What should you use instead?
options: `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY`, which builds without blocking inserts/updates/deletes
`REINDEX TABLE` first, then `CREATE INDEX`
`VACUUM FULL` before creating the index
Create the index inside a long transaction so it can roll back
dbms-ops-security:3.explanation: Plain CREATE INDEX takes a SHARE lock that blocks writes for the whole build. CONCURRENTLY uses a weaker lock and scans twice, taking longer but allowing writes. VACUUM FULL takes an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock and makes things worse.

dbms-ops-security:3.prompt: In PostgreSQL 16, which `ALTER TABLE` on a 500M-row table forces a full table rewrite?
options: ADD COLUMN score int DEFAULT 0
ADD COLUMN note text (nullable, no default)
DROP COLUMN legacy_flag
ADD COLUMN public_id uuid DEFAULT gen_random_uuid()
dbms-ops-security:3.explanation: Since PostgreSQL 11, a non-volatile default is stored in the catalog and applied lazily, so the first two are metadata-only, and DROP COLUMN just marks the column dropped. gen_random_uuid() is volatile, so every row needs its own value and the table is rewritten.

dbms-ops-security:3.prompt: A tiny `ALTER TABLE orders ADD COLUMN ...` migration hangs, and within seconds every query on `orders` times out. What's the likely mechanism and mitigation?
options: The ALTER is rewriting the table; add more IOPS
Autovacuum is holding an exclusive lock; disable autovacuum during deploys
The ALTER waits for ACCESS EXCLUSIVE behind a long-running transaction, and all later queries queue behind it; set a short `lock_timeout` and retry
The connection pool is exhausted by the migration tool; increase pool size
dbms-ops-security:3.explanation: Lock requests queue in order: a pending ACCESS EXCLUSIVE request blocks new readers too. A short lock_timeout makes the migration fail fast and retry instead of stalling traffic. Autovacuum yields to conflicting locks, and a metadata-only ADD COLUMN isn't a rewrite.

dbms-ops-security:3.prompt: In PostgreSQL, why add a constraint as `CHECK (email IS NOT NULL) NOT VALID` and later run `VALIDATE CONSTRAINT` instead of adding it in one step?
options: NOT VALID constraints are never enforced, which is faster
Adding NOT VALID is instant and enforces new writes; VALIDATE scans existing rows under a weaker lock that still allows reads and writes
VALIDATE runs in the background after the transaction commits
It's required because CHECK constraints can't be added to non-empty tables
dbms-ops-security:3.explanation: NOT VALID skips checking existing rows but enforces the constraint for new and updated rows. VALIDATE CONSTRAINT then takes only a SHARE UPDATE EXCLUSIVE lock. A one-step add scans the table while holding a lock that blocks writes.

dbms-ops-security:3.prompt: A release removes the code that reads `users.legacy_score` and, in the same deploy, a migration drops that column. During the rolling deploy, errors spike. Why?
options: Old instances still running the previous code query the dropped column until they're replaced
DROP COLUMN rewrites the table and locks it for minutes
The ORM caches the schema forever
PostgreSQL forbids dropping columns that have data
dbms-ops-security:3.explanation: Code and schema changes must be backward compatible across the deploy window. Drop the column in a later release after no running code references it. DROP COLUMN in PostgreSQL is a fast catalog change, not a rewrite.

dbms-ops-security:3.prompt: Why keep schema changes as versioned migration files in source control, tracked by a migrations table in each database?
options: So the ORM can skip creating indexes
So migrations run faster than manual SQL
So production can be changed without code review
So every environment applies the same changes in the same order exactly once, and the schema history is reviewable
dbms-ops-security:3.explanation: Versioned migrations make schema state reproducible and auditable; the tracking table records what each environment has applied. Speed isn't the point, and they should go through review like any code.

dbms-ops-security:3.prompt: In PostgreSQL, which operations are generally safe to run on a large, busy table without long write-blocking locks? Select all that apply.
options: CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY
ADD COLUMN that is nullable with no default
ADD FOREIGN KEY ... NOT VALID, then VALIDATE later
ALTER COLUMN id TYPE bigint (from int)
VACUUM FULL
dbms-ops-security:3.explanation: Concurrent index builds, metadata-only column adds and NOT VALID constraints avoid long blocking. Changing int to bigint rewrites the table under ACCESS EXCLUSIVE, and VACUUM FULL also rewrites with an exclusive lock.

dbms-ops-security:3.prompt: You must backfill a new column for 200M rows in production. Which practices are sound? Select all that apply.
options: Update in small batches, each in its own short transaction
Throttle and monitor replication lag and lock waits while it runs
Make the backfill idempotent so it can be stopped and resumed
Run one UPDATE over all rows in a single transaction for atomicity
dbms-ops-security:3.explanation: Small resumable batches limit lock duration, WAL bursts and replica lag. A single giant UPDATE holds locks for a long time, generates massive WAL and dead tuples, and loses all progress if it fails.

dbms-ops-security:3.prompt: In PostgreSQL, `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY` can be run inside an explicit transaction block.
options: True
False
dbms-ops-security:3.explanation: False. It cannot run inside a transaction block, which matters for migration tools that wrap each migration in a transaction; such migrations need to opt out of the wrapper.

dbms-ops-security:3.prompt: If `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY` fails partway in PostgreSQL, it can leave behind an INVALID index that must be dropped or rebuilt.
options: True
False
dbms-ops-security:3.explanation: True. A failed concurrent build (e.g. a uniqueness violation) leaves an invalid index that is ignored for reads but still maintained on writes. Drop it and retry, or REINDEX CONCURRENTLY.

dbms-ops-security:4.prompt: The business says: 'We can lose at most 5 minutes of data and be down at most 1 hour after a disaster.' How do these map to recovery objectives?
options: RTO = 5 minutes, RPO = 1 hour
RPO = 5 minutes, RTO = 1 hour
Both describe RPO at different severities
SLA = 5 minutes, SLO = 1 hour
dbms-ops-security:4.explanation: RPO (recovery point objective) is how much data loss is acceptable, measured back in time; RTO (recovery time objective) is how long restoring service may take. Swapping them is the classic mix-up.

dbms-ops-security:4.prompt: What does point-in-time recovery (PITR) in PostgreSQL need?
options: A nightly pg_dump file
A logical replication slot on the primary
A physical base backup plus a continuous archive of WAL files from that backup onward, replayed to a target time
Two synchronous replicas
dbms-ops-security:4.explanation: PITR restores a base backup and replays archived WAL up to `recovery_target_time` (or an LSN/xid). A pg_dump is a logical snapshot of one moment and can't roll forward to arbitrary times.

dbms-ops-security:4.prompt: A teammate says, 'We have a streaming replica, so we don't need backups.' Why is that wrong?
options: Replicas use a different storage format that can't be restored
Replicas can't be promoted to primary
Replicas lag too much to be useful in a disaster
A destructive mistake like `DROP TABLE` replicates to the replica within seconds, so there's nothing to restore from
dbms-ops-security:4.explanation: Replication protects against hardware/node failure, not logical errors or malicious changes, which are faithfully copied. Backups (ideally with PITR) let you go back in time. Replicas can be promoted, which is their purpose.

dbms-ops-security:4.prompt: A 2 TB PostgreSQL database is protected only by a nightly pg_dump. What is the biggest weakness?
options: Up to ~24 hours of data loss, no point-in-time recovery, and a very slow restore that has to reload data and rebuild every index
pg_dump locks all tables exclusively while it runs
pg_dump output can't be restored into a newer PostgreSQL version
pg_dump doesn't include table data, only schema
dbms-ops-security:4.explanation: Logical dumps capture one moment and restore by replaying SQL/COPY then rebuilding indexes, which takes hours at this size. pg_dump uses a consistent MVCC snapshot without blocking writes, and dumps restore fine into newer versions.

dbms-ops-security:4.prompt: Which practice most increases confidence that backups will actually work in an incident?
options: Storing backups in two regions
Regularly restoring backups into a scratch environment and verifying data and timing
Enabling compression on backup files
Checking that backup jobs report exit code 0
dbms-ops-security:4.explanation: Only a real restore proves backups are complete, readable and fast enough for your RTO. Multi-region copies and successful job exit codes are good, but a corrupted or incomplete backup still 'succeeds' until you try restoring it.

dbms-ops-security:4.prompt: At 14:32:10 an engineer ran `DELETE FROM orders` with no WHERE clause in production PostgreSQL; new orders have kept arriving since. With PITR available, what's the best recovery?
options: Restore production in place to 14:32:09, discarding everything after
Restore the latest nightly dump over production
Use PITR to restore a separate instance to just before 14:32:10, extract the deleted rows, and reinsert them into production
Run VACUUM to undelete the rows
dbms-ops-security:4.explanation: Recovering a side instance avoids throwing away valid writes made after the mistake. Rolling production back in place loses those orders, and the nightly dump loses even more. VACUUM removes dead tuples; it never restores them.

dbms-ops-security:4.prompt: Ransomware using stolen admin credentials deleted both the database and the backups stored in the same cloud account. What would have prevented losing the backups?
options: More frequent snapshots
Encrypting the backups with the database's key
Compressing backups so they're quicker to copy
Immutable (object-lock/WORM) backup copies in a separate account the production admins can't delete
dbms-ops-security:4.explanation: Backups must survive the same compromise as production: isolated accounts plus immutability stop deletion even with admin rights. Frequency and encryption don't help if the attacker can delete every copy.

dbms-ops-security:4.prompt: Which are required to perform point-in-time recovery in PostgreSQL? Select all that apply.
options: A physical base backup
Every archived WAL segment from that base backup up to the target
A recovery target (e.g. recovery_target_time) in the restore configuration
A recent pg_dump of the same database
A logical replication slot
dbms-ops-security:4.explanation: PITR = base backup + an unbroken WAL chain + a target to stop at. A single missing WAL segment stops replay at that point. pg_dump and logical slots are separate mechanisms not used by physical PITR.

dbms-ops-security:4.prompt: Which factors directly increase the time a PITR restore takes (pushing up RTO)? Select all that apply.
options: Size of the base backup to download and restore
Volume of WAL generated since that base backup that must be replayed
Throughput from backup storage to the restore host
Number of read replicas attached to production
The chosen RPO target
dbms-ops-security:4.explanation: Restore time is copying the base backup plus replaying WAL, both limited by bandwidth and I/O. Production replicas aren't involved in the restore, and RPO describes acceptable data loss rather than restore duration.

dbms-ops-security:4.prompt: Taking base backups more often shortens PITR restores, because less WAL has to be replayed to reach a recent target time.
options: True
False
dbms-ops-security:4.explanation: True. Replay starts from the nearest earlier base backup; more frequent base backups shorten the WAL chain, trading extra storage and backup I/O for a lower RTO.

dbms-ops-security:4.prompt: Any snapshot of a running database's disk volume is a consistent, restorable backup, however and whenever it is taken.
options: True
False
dbms-ops-security:4.explanation: False. Snapshots must be crash-consistent (atomic across all volumes holding data and WAL) or coordinated with the database (e.g. a backup mode). Snapshotting multiple volumes at different moments can produce an unrecoverable copy.

dbms-ops-security:5.prompt: Which permission setup best follows least privilege for a Node API's PostgreSQL role?
options: SELECT/INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE on the app's tables only; schema migrations run under a separate role with DDL rights
Superuser, so migrations and the app share one connection string
Owner of every table so it can create indexes when needed
Read-only access, with writes going through a superuser connection pool
dbms-ops-security:5.explanation: The runtime role should only do the DML it needs; DDL belongs to a migration role used at deploy time. A superuser or owner role turns any injection or credential leak into full control, including dropping tables or bypassing RLS.

dbms-ops-security:5.prompt: Compliance requires a record of every read of the `salaries` table in PostgreSQL. What is purpose-built for this?
options: Setting `log_min_duration_statement = 0`
A trigger on SELECT that inserts into an audit table
The pgAudit extension with object-level auditing on that table
Enabling pg_stat_statements
dbms-ops-security:5.explanation: pgAudit produces structured audit log entries, and object audit logging can target specific relations and statement classes like READ. PostgreSQL has no SELECT triggers, and pg_stat_statements aggregates normalized query stats without per-user, per-access records.

dbms-ops-security:5.prompt: Every engineer and service connects as the same `postgres` superuser. After a table is wrongly altered, the logs don't help. Why?
options: PostgreSQL doesn't log DDL
Superuser statements are excluded from logs
Logs are only kept for 24 hours
Shared credentials make every action look like the same identity, so nothing can be attributed to a person or service
dbms-ops-security:5.explanation: Auditing depends on distinct identities. Separate roles per person and per service (ideally short-lived credentials) make logs attributable and permissions targeted. PostgreSQL can log DDL for all users including superusers.

dbms-ops-security:5.prompt: Auditors worry that DBAs could quietly delete audit records of their own actions. What best addresses this?
options: Store audit logs in a table only the DBAs can modify
Ship audit events to an append-only, separate log store the database admins have no write/delete rights to
Encrypt the audit table with the DBA's key
Rotate audit logs daily
dbms-ops-security:5.explanation: Audit trails need separation of duties: the people being audited must not be able to alter the record. An external, write-once sink provides that. Keeping logs in a table the DBAs control defeats the purpose.

dbms-ops-security:5.prompt: In PostgreSQL, a multi-tenant table has ROW LEVEL SECURITY enabled with a tenant policy, yet the app still sees every tenant's rows. The app connects as the table's owner. Why?
options: Policies only apply to UPDATE and DELETE
RLS requires the pgAudit extension
Table owners bypass RLS unless `ALTER TABLE ... FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY` is set (and superusers/BYPASSRLS roles always bypass it)
The policy must be created before the table's data is inserted
dbms-ops-security:5.explanation: By default, RLS doesn't apply to the table owner. Use a separate non-owner app role or FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY. Policies can apply to SELECT, and they work regardless of when rows were inserted.

dbms-ops-security:5.prompt: In PostgreSQL you ran `GRANT SELECT ON ALL TABLES IN SCHEMA app TO reporting;`. A month later, reporting gets 'permission denied' on a new table. Why, and what's the fix?
options: The grant only covered tables that existed then; use `ALTER DEFAULT PRIVILEGES ... GRANT SELECT ON TABLES TO reporting` for future tables
Grants expire after 30 days unless renewed
New tables are created in a different schema by default
The reporting role needs superuser to read new tables
dbms-ops-security:5.explanation: GRANT ... ON ALL TABLES is a one-time action over existing objects. Default privileges (set for the role that creates tables) apply grants automatically to future objects. Grants don't expire, and superuser would violate least privilege.

dbms-ops-security:5.prompt: What's the main risk of turning on full statement logging with bound parameters for every query in production?
options: The database will refuse connections once logs exceed 1 GB
Sensitive values such as tokens, emails or card numbers end up in logs that many more people and systems can read
Logs make queries non-deterministic
Logging disables prepared statements
dbms-ops-security:5.explanation: Logs are often shipped widely and retained long, so they become a secondary store of sensitive data. Audit what happened and by whom, and redact or avoid parameter values. Logging doesn't change query semantics.

dbms-ops-security:5.prompt: Which practices support least privilege for databases? Select all that apply.
options: Separate roles for the app, migrations and read-only analytics
Short-lived credentials (e.g. IAM database auth or dynamically issued secrets)
Granting only the specific tables and operations each role needs
Giving the app role superuser so on-call fixes are faster
Sharing a single role across all microservices to simplify rotation
dbms-ops-security:5.explanation: Narrow roles and short-lived credentials limit blast radius and make access attributable. Superuser for the app and one shared role across services both expand the damage of any single compromise.

dbms-ops-security:5.prompt: Which fields make a database audit log entry useful for an investigation? Select all that apply.
options: The authenticated identity (user or service role)
The action and object (e.g. UPDATE on payroll.salaries)
An accurate timestamp
Source details such as client address or application name
The full plaintext card number from the statement
dbms-ops-security:5.explanation: Who, what, when and from where let you reconstruct events. Copying sensitive values into the audit log creates a new exposure and a compliance problem; record identifiers instead.

dbms-ops-security:5.prompt: Since PostgreSQL 15, ordinary roles no longer have CREATE privilege on the `public` schema by default.
options: True
False
dbms-ops-security:5.explanation: True. PostgreSQL 15 revoked CREATE on `public` from PUBLIC for new databases, closing a long-standing hole where any user could create objects in the default search path.

dbms-ops-security:5.prompt: In PostgreSQL, you cannot grant a role SELECT on a view without also granting it SELECT on the view's underlying tables.
options: True
False
dbms-ops-security:5.explanation: False. By default a view accesses its base tables with the view owner's privileges, so you can expose only certain columns/rows through it. (Views created with security_invoker = true check the caller's privileges instead.)
